title: Morris v. Sparrow
lead: A ranch worker trains the horse he says was promised as compensation, then seeks that animal despite the owner’s claim of unsatisfactory work and a final wage check marked paid in full.

actors.name: Archie Sparrow
actors.role: Cowboy and experienced trainer seeking Keno as promised ranch-work compensation.

actors.name: C. L. “Chip” Morris
actors.role: Ranch and horse owner contesting Sparrow’s entitlement and equitable remedy.

actors.name: Keno
actors.role: Initially unbroken brown horse trained by Sparrow into a promising roping horse.

proceedings: The chancellor heard testimony and ordered Morris to deliver Keno.
The Arkansas Supreme Court affirmed February 20, 1956; rehearing was denied March 26.
limits: The performance condition was resolved on evidence, not pleadings. The decree transferred the horse, awarded no separate training fee, and imposed no ongoing personal-service duty. The final-check ruling concerns these circumstances, not a general denial of settlement notations’ effect.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A rodeo acquaintance becomes a sixteen-week ranch arrangement
sections.cue: What compensation did each side describe?
paragraphs: Archie Sparrow, an experienced cowboy and horse trainer, met C. L. “Chip” Morris through rodeo activities in Florida. They planned to travel to Morris’s Arkansas ranch and then Canada but changed course: Morris would go to Canada while Sparrow remained to perform ranch work.

They agreed to sixteen weeks for $400 cash. Sparrow maintained that compensation also included Keno, Morris’s brown horse. Morris acknowledged a possible transfer but insisted it depended on satisfactory ranch work and claimed Sparrow fell short.

Keno was essentially unbroken when Sparrow arrived. In spare time, Sparrow trained him into a horse that, with a little more work, could become a first-class roping horse. That particular investment later supported Sparrow’s request for Keno himself rather than money.

sections.title: The parties settle the cash balance but continue disagreeing about Keno
sections.cue: Why did cashing the check not necessarily settle everything?
paragraphs: After sixteen weeks, both agreed $167 remained of the cash pay. At a bank, Morris handed Sparrow a check for exactly that amount bearing a notation that labor had been paid in full. Sparrow cashed it while continuing to insist on the horse.

At the same encounter, Morris offered Keno subject to a new restriction against sale or disposal. Sparrow rejected that restriction. Their discussions showed agreement on the outstanding money alongside a continuing horse dispute, rather than an undisputed comprehensive settlement.

sections.title: The chancellor orders delivery after hearing the parties
sections.cue: How did the appeal distinguish entitlement from remedy?
paragraphs: Sparrow filed in chancery for specific performance, and the chancellor ordered Morris to deliver Keno. Morris appealed, contesting satisfaction of the work condition, equitable relief for personal property, and survival of the claim after the check.

The Supreme Court recognized the chancellor’s superior opportunity to assess both witnesses. It found no basis to deem the determination for Sparrow against the preponderance of evidence. This was review of a factual resolution after testimony, not acceptance of unproved allegations or invalidation of satisfaction clauses generally. The opinion supplied no broad objective-or-subjective satisfaction test.

Entitlement and remedy remained separate. Training did not create a right to a horse never promised, while a promise alone would not establish that money was inadequate. The affirmed factual finding supplied the first question; the horse’s particular value supplied the second.

sources.pinpoint: 287 S.W.2d at 584–586; Procedural history; Performance condition; Use in class

sections.title: Sparrow’s work makes this horse’s delivery an appropriate equitable remedy
sections.cue: Why could an appraisable animal still warrant specific performance?
paragraphs: Justice Robinson accepted that damages ordinarily remedied a promise to deliver personal property but found special circumstances. Sparrow’s time and skill transformed this green horse into a roping prospect with peculiar value to him. Paying market price would not necessarily reproduce the relationship between that work, this animal, and the promised compensation.

The reasoning did not require that Keno be incapable of valuation or make every horse unique for every claimant. The question was adequacy of money for this promised performance. Sparrow’s services were already complete; the decree required property transfer rather than continued labor.

Arkansas Statutes § 68-1468 further authorized equity to order delivery of specific or ascertained goods when appropriate. Identification of the goods did not make relief automatic; the particular circumstances explaining damages’ inadequacy remained essential.

sources.pinpoint: 287 S.W.2d at 584–585; Equitable and statutory reasoning

sections.title: The final check pays a conceded item without replacing the horse obligation
sections.cue: What facts defeat accord and satisfaction?
paragraphs: Accord and satisfaction required acceptance of a proposed settlement, not merely words on a check divorced from context. The check paid exactly the undisputed cash balance. Sparrow continued claiming Keno, and Morris himself discussed delivery subject to a rejected additional restriction. The evidence did not establish agreed substitution for the whole compensation package.

The court acknowledged that a disputed money amount knowingly tendered and accepted in full settlement could differ. It did not adjudicate that hypothetical or deprive all restrictive notations of effect. It examined the paid obligation, remaining dispute, and contemporaneous conduct.

On February 20, 1956, the Supreme Court of Arkansas affirmed delivery of Keno. It substituted no damages award, ordered no new trial, and awarded no separate training fee. Rehearing was denied March 26 without a second merits opinion; no concurrence or dissent was reported.

sources.pinpoint: 287 S.W.2d at 585–586; Accord and satisfaction; Actual judgment; Separate opinions
